sections.heading: Age-Related Pharmacokinetic & Pharmacodynamic Changes: Why Older Adults Are Uniquely Vulnerable
points: ABSORPTION: Gastric pH rises with aging (reduced parietal cell mass), slowing dissolution of weakly acidic drugs (e.g., ketoconazole, iron salts). Reduced splanchnic blood flow and GI motility delay Tmax but overall bioavailability is generally preserved — this is the one PK parameter LEAST affected by aging.

DISTRIBUTION: Total body water decreases 10-15% while adipose tissue increases 20-40% from age 25 to 75. Hydrophilic drugs (digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides) have SMALLER Vd → higher peak plasma concentrations at standard doses. Lipophilic drugs (diazepam, amiodarone) have LARGER Vd → prolonged half-life and accumulation. Albumin drops ~15-20%, increasing free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs (warfarin, phenytoin, valproate).

METABOLISM: Hepatic mass declines ~25-35% and hepatic blood flow drops ~40% by age 65. Phase I reactions (CYP-mediated oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) are significantly impaired; Phase II reactions (glucuronidation, acetylation, sulfation) are relatively preserved. This is why lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam (LOT — all Phase II only) are preferred benzodiazepines in older adults if absolutely needed.

ELIMINATION: GFR declines ~0.75 mL/min/year after age 40 even without CKD; by age 80, average GFR is 50-60 mL/min. Serum creatinine may appear normal despite significantly reduced GFR due to decreased muscle mass — always calculate CrCl (Cockcroft-Gault) or use CKD-EPI. Renally cleared drugs (DOACs, gabapentin, metformin, digoxin) require dose adjustment.

PHARMACODYNAMICS: Increased sensitivity of the CNS to sedatives, anticholinergics, and opioids due to reduced cholinergic neurons, decreased dopaminergic tone, and blood-brain barrier permeability changes. Baroreceptor reflex blunting increases susceptibility to orthostatic hypotension from alpha-blockers, diuretics, and vasodilators. Reduced beta-receptor sensitivity (downregulation) diminishes response to beta-agonists and beta-blockers.

ANTICHOLINERGIC BURDEN: The cumulative effect of multiple medications with anticholinergic properties (diphenhydramine + oxybutynin + paroxetine) is additive. Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scale quantifies risk. High cumulative ACB scores independently predict delirium, cognitive decline, falls, and mortality. Cholinergic deficit in aging brain means even low-grade anticholinergic exposure has outsized impact.

NET EFFECT: These physiologic changes create a narrow therapeutic index for many drugs in older adults, making standard adult dosing inherently risky. The adage 'start low, go slow, but go' applies — but the corollary is equally important: 'deprescribe when the risk-benefit shifts.'
sections.teaching_pearl: The LOT drugs (Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) bypass Phase I hepatic metabolism entirely via glucuronidation (Phase II), making them the 'safer' benzodiazepines in older adults — but per Beers 2023, ALL benzodiazepines are still potentially inappropriate regardless of metabolism route.
sections.board_tip: Board question classic: Elderly patient on phenytoin with low albumin — always correct the phenytoin level using the Sheiner-Tozer equation. A 'normal' total phenytoin level may actually represent a toxic free level when albumin is low.

sections.heading: Beers Criteria & STOPP/START: The Screening Tools and How to Apply Them
points: BEERS CRITERIA (AGS 2023): Five categories — (1) PIMs to avoid in most older adults, (2) PIMs to avoid in certain diseases/syndromes, (3) drugs to use with caution, (4) drug-drug interactions to avoid, (5) dose adjustments based on renal function. Major updates in 2023 include refined guidance on PPIs, added warnings on long-term NSAID use, and clarified sulfonylurea recommendations.

HIGH-YIELD BEERS MEDICATIONS: First-gen antihistamines (diphenhydramine — strong anticholinergic), long-acting sulfonylureas (glyburide — hypoglycemia risk), skeletal muscle relaxants (cyclobenzaprine, metaxalone — sedation, anticholinergic), sliding scale insulin in non-ICU settings (hypoglycemia without benefit), peripheral alpha-1 blockers for hypertension (doxazosin — orthostasis, falls).

STOPP/START CRITERIA (Version 3, 2023): STOPP = Screening Tool of Older Persons' Prescriptions (identifies PIMs to STOP); START = Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatment (identifies beneficial drugs being OMITTED). STOPP/START is more condition-specific than Beers and has stronger evidence for reducing ADEs in European trials. Includes 190 STOPP and 44 START criteria.

STOPP EXAMPLES: Stop long-acting benzodiazepines if fall risk, stop PPIs beyond 8 weeks without clear indication, stop loop diuretics for ankle edema without heart failure, stop anticholinergics in patients with dementia or chronic constipation, stop duplicate drug classes (two ACE inhibitors, two SSRIs).

START EXAMPLES: START statins in documented atherosclerotic CVD if life expectancy >3 years, START vitamin D/calcium in osteoporosis, START ACE inhibitor in HFrEF, START laxatives in patients on chronic opioids, START beta-blockers in stable angina. These omissions of beneficial therapy are as harmful as inappropriate prescriptions — the 'prescribing omission' concept.

COMPARISON: Beers is US-focused (AGS), widely used for quality metrics, but is sometimes criticized as a 'blacklist' that doesn't account for individual patient context. STOPP/START is used internationally, more explicit about indication-driven decisions, and has shown reduction in ADEs in the SENATOR and OPTI-SCRIPT trials. Both are screening tools, NOT absolute contraindications — clinical judgment remains paramount.
LIMITATIONS: Neither tool fully addresses patient goals of care, functional status, or remaining life expectancy. Deprescribing requires a broader framework than simply applying a checklist.
sections.teaching_pearl: STOPP/START has something Beers does not: the START component. Prescribing omissions (e.g., not starting an anticoagulant in AFib, not starting a bisphosphonate after hip fracture) cause as much morbidity as PIMs. Always look for undertreated conditions alongside overtreated ones.
sections.board_tip: Board favorite: 78-year-old with insomnia started on diphenhydramine who then develops urinary retention and confusion. This is the classic anticholinergic toxicity cascade (peripheral: urinary retention, dry mouth; central: delirium). Diphenhydramine is on Beers as 'avoid in most older adults.' The answer is always to STOP the offending drug first.

sections.heading: Deprescribing: Systematic Approach, Evidence, and Practical Framework
points: DEFINITION: Deprescribing is the planned, supervised process of dose reduction or discontinuation of medications that are no longer beneficial or may be causing harm, in the context of an individual patient's current goals of care, functional status, and life expectancy. It is NOT simply stopping medications abruptly.

5-STEP DEPRESCRIBING FRAMEWORK (Scott et al.): (1) Ascertain all current medications and indications, (2) Consider overall fall/ADR risk using tools like anticholinergic burden scales, (3) Assess each drug for appropriateness using Beers/STOPP/START, (4) Prioritize drugs to discontinue (highest harm, lowest benefit first), (5) Implement a gradual taper plan with close monitoring for withdrawal or disease recurrence.

EVIDENCE — LANDMARK TRIALS: The EMPOWER trial (2014) showed a direct-to-patient educational brochure about benzodiazepine risks led to 27% complete discontinuation at 6 months vs 5% in controls — empowering patients works. The OPTI-SCRIPT RCT demonstrated pharmacist-physician collaborative medication review reduced PIMs by 25%. Garfinkel (2010) showed systematic deprescribing of a mean of 4.4 drugs per patient resulted in 88% success rate with improved mortality and cognition.

TAPER STRATEGIES BY DRUG CLASS: PPIs — step down to H2RA or reduce to lowest effective dose over 2-4 weeks (rebound acid hypersecretion if stopped abruptly). Benzodiazepines — reduce dose by 10-25% every 1-2 weeks (withdrawal seizures if stopped abruptly). SSRIs — taper over 4+ weeks to prevent discontinuation syndrome (dizziness, paresthesias, flu-like symptoms). Opioids — reduce by 10% every 1-4 weeks. Antihypertensives — reduce one agent at a time, monitor BP closely.

DRUGS TO DEPRESCRIBE FIRST (highest yield, most evidence): PPIs without clear indication beyond 8 weeks, benzodiazepines and Z-drugs for insomnia, anticholinergic medications especially if cumulative burden is high, duplicate therapies, and medications for conditions that have resolved or where treatment targets have shifted with limited life expectancy (e.g., aggressive diabetes control with A1c target <7% in a frail 85-year-old).

GOALS-OF-CARE INTEGRATION: Time-to-benefit is a critical concept. Statins take 2-5 years for NNT benefit; in patients with life expectancy <1-2 years, the burden (myalgias, pill burden, drug interactions) may outweigh benefit. Bisphosphonates take 12-18 months for fracture reduction benefit. Conversely, anticoagulants and analgesics have immediate benefit and should generally be continued.

BARRIERS TO DEPRESCRIBING: Patient reluctance ('but I've been on this for 20 years'), fear of disease recurrence, prescriber inertia, fragmented care across multiple specialists, and lack of structured deprescribing protocols in health systems. Shared decision-making and patient education are the most evidence-based solutions to overcome these barriers.
sections.teaching_pearl: The 'prescribing cascade' is a key concept: Drug A causes side effect → Side effect is misdiagnosed as a new condition → Drug B is prescribed to treat the side effect → Drug B causes its own side effects. Classic example: NSAID → hypertension → amlodipine → pedal edema → furosemide → hypokalemia → potassium supplement. Recognizing the cascade is the first step to effective deprescribing.
sections.board_tip: When a board question describes an elderly patient with a NEW symptom after starting a medication, always consider that the new symptom IS a drug adverse effect (the prescribing cascade), not a new disease. The correct answer is almost always to stop the offending drug, not to add a new one.

summary_points: Age-related pharmacokinetic changes — decreased renal clearance, reduced hepatic Phase I metabolism, increased adipose distribution, lower albumin — narrow the therapeutic index and mandate dose adjustments; always calculate GFR rather than relying on serum creatinine alone in older adults.

The anticholinergic burden is cumulative and additive: combining even mildly anticholinergic drugs (paroxetine + oxybutynin + diphenhydramine) creates a high ACB score that independently predicts delirium, cognitive decline, falls, and mortality in older adults.

Beers Criteria (AGS 2023) identifies PIMs across five categories; STOPP/START (v3, 2023) adds the crucial dimension of prescribing omissions (START criteria) — beneficial drugs being withheld are as harmful as inappropriate drugs being given.

Deprescribing is a systematic, supervised, patient-centered process — not simply stopping drugs. High-yield first targets include PPIs beyond 8 weeks without indication, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, and medications whose time-to-benefit exceeds life expectancy.

The prescribing cascade (Drug A side effect → misdiagnosed as new disease → Drug B added) is the single most testable and clinically important concept in geriatric pharmacology. Always ask 'could this new symptom be a drug side effect?' before adding another medication.

The EMPOWER trial demonstrated that patient education alone achieves 27% benzodiazepine discontinuation — shared decision-making and patient empowerment are evidence-based strategies that overcome barriers to deprescribing.

question.stem: A 58-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of worsening dyspnea on exertion and palpitations over the past 3 weeks. He was diagnosed with atrial fibrillation 10 months ago at an urgent care visit, at which time he was started on apixaban and metoprolol. He reports that his symptoms have progressively worsened despite taking metoprolol 50 mg twice daily, and he now becomes short of breath walking one block. He has a history of hypertension treated with lisinopril and type 2 diabetes managed with metformin. He does not smoke and drinks 1-2 glasses of wine per week. His temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, heart rate is 112 beats/min and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. BMI is 29 kg/m2. Physical examination reveals an irregularly irregular rhythm, jugular venous distension to 10 cm H2O, bibasilar crackles one-third up the lung fields, and trace bilateral lower extremity edema. An electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 114 beats/min and no ST-segment changes. Transthoracic echocardiography shows a left ventricular ejection fraction of 35%, moderate left atrial dilation (4.6 cm), and no significant valvular disease. Serum TSH is 2.1 mIU/L, creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL, NT-proBNP is 2,800 pg/mL, and hemoglobin is 13.8 g/dL. After initiation of intravenous diuresis and guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, his volume status improves but he remains in atrial fibrillation with a heart rate of 92 beats/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of his atrial fibrillation?

choices.text: Continue rate control with metoprolol alone
Add digoxin for additional rate control
Referral for catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation

question.explanation: Per the 2023 ACC/AHA AFib guideline, early rhythm control is recommended for patients with AF diagnosed within the past 12 months, particularly those with symptomatic AF and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). The EAST-AFNET 4 trial demonstrated that early rhythm control (within 1 year of AF diagnosis) reduced the composite of cardiovascular death, stroke, and hospitalization for heart failure or acute coronary syndrome compared with rate control alone. Furthermore, the CASTLE-AF trial specifically showed that catheter ablation in patients with symptomatic AF and HFrEF (LVEF <=35%) significantly reduced all-cause mortality and heart failure hospitalizations compared with medical therapy. The CABANA trial also showed benefit of ablation in intention-to-treat and particularly in the as-treated analysis. This patient has AF diagnosed 10 months ago (within 12 months), symptomatic HFrEF (LVEF 35%), and remains symptomatic despite adequate rate control (HR 92 bpm) and initiation of HF GDMT, making catheter ablation the most appropriate rhythm control strategy. Rate control alone (A, B) fails to leverage the mortality benefit demonstrated in EAST-AFNET 4 and CASTLE-AF for this population. Flecainide (D) is contraindicated in structural heart disease and HFrEF. Dronedarone (E) is contraindicated in NYHA class III-IV HF and recently decompensated HF (per BLACK-BOX warning from the ANDROMEDA trial).

wrong_explanations.why: Rate control alone was inferior to early rhythm control in EAST-AFNET 4 for AF diagnosed within 12 months. In symptomatic AF with HFrEF, rhythm control with ablation reduces mortality per CASTLE-AF, making rate control alone suboptimal.

Adding digoxin addresses rate control only. His ventricular rate is already 92 bpm on metoprolol. The primary issue is persistent AF contributing to HFrEF, which requires rhythm control, not more aggressive rate control.

Flecainide (class IC antiarrhythmic) is contraindicated in patients with structural heart disease and reduced LVEF due to proarrhythmic risk, as demonstrated in the CAST trial. It should never be used with HFrEF.

Dronedarone is contraindicated in patients with NYHA III-IV heart failure or recent decompensation. The ANDROMEDA trial showed increased mortality with dronedarone in decompensated HF, leading to a black-box warning.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Atrial Fibrillation: Rate versus Rhythm Control in HFrEF

board_pearls: EAST-AFNET 4 demonstrated that early rhythm control within 12 months of AF diagnosis reduces cardiovascular death, stroke, and HF hospitalization; this benefit is strongest when rhythm control is initiated early rather than deferred.

Per the 2023 ACC/AHA AFib guideline, catheter ablation receives a Class 1 recommendation for symptomatic AF in patients with HFrEF, supported by CASTLE-AF showing reduced all-cause mortality and HF hospitalizations versus medical therapy.

The key discriminator between catheter ablation and continued rate control is the presence of HFrEF with recently diagnosed AF; rate control alone misses the mortality benefit demonstrated when rhythm is restored in this specific population.

CASTLE-AF enrolled patients with LVEF <=35% and symptomatic AF; ablation reduced the primary composite of death or HF hospitalization by 38%, with the benefit driven by both components. CABANA showed ablation benefit particularly in the as-treated analysis across AF subtypes.

The most common trap is choosing dronedarone for rhythm control in HFrEF; dronedarone is contraindicated in NYHA III-IV or recent decompensation (ANDROMEDA trial showed doubled mortality), and flecainide is contraindicated in any structural heart disease (CAST trial).
teaching_points: The older AFFIRM trial (2002) found no mortality benefit of rhythm control, but used older antiarrhythmics and enrolled older patients with longstanding AF; EAST-AFNET 4 (2020) changed practice by showing early rhythm control benefits when initiated within 12 months of diagnosis.

In AF with HFrEF, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy should be considered; restoration of sinus rhythm via catheter ablation may substantially improve LVEF and is preferred over antiarrhythmic drugs in this population.

Antiarrhythmic drug selection in AF is critically dependent on comorbidities: amiodarone is the only antiarrhythmic safe in HFrEF (but has significant toxicity), flecainide and propafenone are contraindicated in structural heart disease, and dronedarone is contraindicated in decompensated or severe HF.
summary_points: Early rhythm control with catheter ablation is the preferred strategy for symptomatic atrial fibrillation diagnosed within 12 months in a patient with HFrEF, supported by EAST-AFNET 4 and CASTLE-AF trial data and endorsed by the 2023 ACC/AHA AFib guideline.

topic: HOCM with syncope — ICD indication and SCD risk stratification

talk.title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy with Syncope
talk.subtitle: ICD Indication and Sudden Cardiac Death Risk Stratification in HCM
guideline_sources: 2020 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Diagnosis and Treatment of Patients with Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
2024 ESC Guidelines on Management of Cardiomyopathies

references.source: 2020 AHA/ACC Guideline for Diagnosis and Treatment of HCM
O'Mahony C et al. A novel clinical risk prediction model for sudden cardiac death in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM Risk-SCD). Eur Heart J. 2014;35(30):2010-20.

question.stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after losing consciousness while playing basketball. He reports sudden onset of lightheadedness followed by brief loss of consciousness lasting approximately 10 seconds, with spontaneous recovery. He denies chest pain, palpitations, tongue biting, or urinary incontinence. He has no prior medical history. His father died suddenly at age 34 during exercise; his paternal uncle had a cardiac defibrillator implanted at age 40. He does not smoke or drink alcohol. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg, heart rate is 68/min, respiratory rate is 14/min, and oxygen saturation is 99% on room air. On cardiac examination, there is a grade III/VI harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur heard best at the left lower sternal border that increases with standing from a squatting position and during the Valsalva maneuver. There is no S3 or S4. Lungs are clear. An electrocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy with deep T-wave inversions in leads V4-V6. Transthoracic echocardiography reveals asymmetric septal hypertrophy with a maximum left ventricular wall thickness of 32 mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve, a resting left ventricular outflow tract gradient of 55 mmHg, left atrial diameter of 48 mm, and a left ventricular ejection fraction of 65%. A 48-hour ambulatory ECG monitor shows three runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, the longest lasting 8 beats at a rate of 180/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: Per the 2020 AHA/ACC HCM Guideline, ICD implantation is recommended (Class I) for HCM patients who have survived a cardiac arrest due to VT/VF, or who have spontaneous sustained VT causing syncope or hemodynamic compromise. For primary prevention, the guideline recommends a shared decision-making approach using established SCD risk factors. This patient has multiple major risk factors: (1) unexplained syncope likely arrhythmic in nature (exertional, brief, without prodrome or postictal features), (2) family history of sudden cardiac death in a first-degree relative younger than 40, (3) massive left ventricular hypertrophy (wall thickness >=30 mm, here 32 mm), and (4) nonsustained ventricular tachycardia on ambulatory monitoring. Having even one of these major risk factors warrants consideration for an ICD, and this patient has four. Per the 2020 AHA/ACC guideline, an ICD is reasonable (Class IIa) for patients with HCM and one or more of these major risk factors when the estimated 5-year SCD risk is judged sufficient after shared decision-making. With this confluence of high-risk features in a young patient, ICD placement is the most appropriate next step. Surgical myectomy addresses symptoms of LVOT obstruction but does not address SCD risk. Beta-blockers manage symptoms but do not prevent SCD. Amiodarone is not recommended as primary SCD prevention in HCM. While cardiac MRI can identify late gadolinium enhancement as an additional risk modifier, it would not change management here given the already compelling indication for ICD.

wrong_explanations.why: Amiodarone is not recommended for primary prevention of SCD in HCM per 2020 AHA/ACC guidelines. It has not been shown to reduce sudden death risk and carries significant long-term toxicity, especially in a young patient.

Septal myectomy is indicated for refractory LVOT obstruction symptoms despite maximally tolerated medical therapy. While this patient has significant obstruction, the immediate priority is SCD prevention with an ICD given multiple high-risk features and syncope.

Beta-blockers are first-line for symptomatic LVOT obstruction and may reduce gradient, but they have not been proven to reduce SCD risk in HCM. This patient's syncope and risk profile mandate ICD, not beta-blocker monotherapy.

Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement is useful as an ancillary risk modifier in borderline cases. However, this patient already has four established major SCD risk factors, making the ICD decision clear without requiring additional imaging to further stratify risk.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: SCD Risk Stratification and ICD Indication

board_pearls: The 2020 AHA/ACC HCM guideline identifies five major SCD risk factors: family history of SCD, massive LVH (>=30 mm), unexplained syncope, nonsustained VT on ambulatory monitoring, and LV apical aneurysm; the presence of any one warrants ICD discussion.

Per the 2020 AHA/ACC guideline, ICD is Class I for secondary prevention (survived VT/VF arrest) and Class IIa for primary prevention when one or more major risk factors are present after shared decision-making regarding estimated 5-year SCD risk.

Unexplained syncope in HCM that is exertional, brief, without prodrome, and lacks features of vasovagal or neurologic etiology is presumed arrhythmic and is a major SCD risk factor, distinguishing it from neurocardiogenic syncope that would not independently warrant an ICD.

The ESC HCM Risk-SCD calculator (O'Mahony et al., 2014) uses age, maximal wall thickness, LA diameter, peak LVOT gradient, family history of SCD, NSVT, and unexplained syncope to generate a 5-year SCD risk score; >=6% favors ICD, 4-6% may be considered, and <4% generally does not.

The most common wrong-answer trap is choosing septal myectomy or beta-blocker therapy, which address LVOT obstruction symptoms but do NOT prevent sudden cardiac death; neither substitutes for an ICD in a patient with established high-risk features.
teaching_points: In HCM, SCD risk stratification is separate from symptom management of LVOT obstruction; ICD is the only intervention proven to prevent SCD.
Maximal wall thickness >=30 mm is one of the strongest individual predictors of SCD in HCM and independently warrants ICD consideration even in asymptomatic patients.

Late gadolinium enhancement on cardiac MRI (>=15% of LV mass) is recognized as an ancillary risk modifier in the 2020 AHA/ACC guideline and may tip the decision in borderline cases, but it does not replace the established five major risk factors.
summary_points: Young patient with HCM and four major SCD risk factors (unexplained exertional syncope, family history of SCD, massive LVH >=30 mm, NSVT) requires ICD implantation as the most appropriate next step per the 2020 AHA/ACC HCM guideline.

topic: Recurrent C. difficile infection — fidaxomicin vs FMT (2024 IDSA)

talk.title: Recurrent C. difficile Infection Management
talk.subtitle: Fidaxomicin vs Fecal Microbiota Transplantation in Recurrent CDI
guideline_sources: IDSA/SHEA 2024 Focused Update: Management of Clostridioides difficile Infection in Adults

references.source: IDSA/SHEA Clinical Practice Guideline Update: Management of Clostridioides difficile Infection in Adults
Johnson S et al. Fidaxomicin versus vancomycin for Clostridium difficile infection (EXTEND trial)
Kelly CR et al. Fecal microbiota transplantation for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (PUNCH CD3)

question.stem: A 72-year-old woman is evaluated in the outpatient infectious disease clinic for recurrent diarrhea. She was treated 3 months ago for an initial episode of Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) with a 10-day course of oral vancomycin 125 mg four times daily. Her symptoms resolved completely. Two weeks after completing vancomycin, she developed watery, non-bloody diarrhea occurring 6-8 times per day with lower abdominal cramping. Stool testing was positive for C. difficile toxin by enzyme immunoassay and nucleic acid amplification. She was treated with a second 10-day course of oral vancomycin followed by a tapered and pulsed regimen over 6 weeks. Her symptoms again resolved but have now recurred 10 days after completing the taper, with 5-7 watery stools per day. Repeat stool C. difficile toxin testing is positive. Her medical history includes hypertension and osteoarthritis. She takes amlodipine and acetaminophen. She does not drink alcohol or smoke. Temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), blood pressure is 134/78 mmHg, heart rate is 82/min, and respiratory rate is 16/min. Abdominal examination reveals mild diffuse tenderness without rebound or guarding. Bowel sounds are hyperactive. Laboratory studies show a white blood cell count of 9,800/microL, creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL, and albumin of 3.4 g/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: Per the 2024 IDSA/SHEA focused update, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) or standardized microbiota-based therapies (e.g., fecal microbiota live-jslm [Rebyota] or fecal microbiota spores live-brpk [Vowst]) are recommended for patients with a second or subsequent recurrence of CDI who have failed appropriate antibiotic therapy. This patient has experienced her second recurrence (third episode total) despite an adequate vancomycin taper-and-pulse regimen, which is the key discriminating feature. The 2024 guidelines position FMT/microbiota restoration as the preferred approach after failure of at least one extended vancomycin regimen for recurrent CDI. Fidaxomicin is preferred over vancomycin for initial and first-recurrence CDI because it has lower recurrence rates (EXTEND trial demonstrated sustained clinical response of approximately 70% vs 59% for vancomycin). However, after a second recurrence following a vancomycin taper, the recurrence risk with any antibiotic-only strategy exceeds 50-60%. FMT achieves sustained cure rates of 80-90% in multiply recurrent CDI. The PUNCH CD3 and similar trials demonstrated superiority of microbiota-based therapies over antibiotics alone for multiply recurrent CDI. Repeating a vancomycin taper would be inappropriate given prior failure. Metronidazole is inferior to vancomycin and fidaxomicin and is not recommended for recurrent CDI. Bezlotoxumab is an adjunctive anti-toxin B monoclonal antibody used alongside antibiotics to reduce recurrence risk, not as standalone therapy.

wrong_explanations.why: Fidaxomicin is preferred over vancomycin for first recurrence but after a second recurrence following a vancomycin taper, the 2024 IDSA/SHEA update recommends microbiota-based therapy (FMT or standardized microbiota products) over another antibiotic-only approach given recurrence rates exceed 50-60%.

A vancomycin taper and pulse was already attempted and failed in this patient. Repeating the same regimen that failed carries a high recurrence risk exceeding 60% and is not recommended by the 2024 IDSA/SHEA update for multiply recurrent CDI.

Metronidazole is inferior to vancomycin and fidaxomicin for CDI treatment. Per IDSA/SHEA guidelines, metronidazole should only be used when vancomycin or fidaxomicin is unavailable. It has no role in recurrent CDI management.

Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody against C. difficile toxin B used as adjunctive therapy alongside antibiotics to reduce recurrence risk. It is not approved or recommended as standalone therapy and does not treat active CDI infection.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection: FMT vs fidaxomicin

board_pearls: Per 2024 IDSA/SHEA, FMT or standardized microbiota-based therapy (Rebyota, Vowst) is recommended after a second or subsequent CDI recurrence that has failed appropriate antibiotic therapy, achieving sustained cure rates of 80-90% versus 40-50% with antibiotics alone.

Fidaxomicin is preferred over vancomycin for initial and first-recurrence CDI per 2024 IDSA/SHEA because it reduces recurrence rates (EXTEND trial: approximately 70% sustained response vs 59% vancomycin), but it is insufficient as monotherapy for multiply recurrent CDI.

The discriminating feature between fidaxomicin and FMT on boards is the number of recurrences: fidaxomicin is best for first recurrence, whereas FMT or standardized microbiota-based therapy is preferred after two or more recurrences or failure of a prior extended vancomycin regimen.

The PUNCH CD3 trial demonstrated that fecal microbiota live-jslm (Rebyota) significantly reduced CDI recurrence compared to placebo at 8 weeks, supporting FDA approval of standardized microbiota products for recurrent CDI in 2023.

The most common wrong-answer trap is choosing fidaxomicin for multiply recurrent CDI; while fidaxomicin reduces recurrence versus vancomycin, its benefit diminishes substantially after two or more recurrences, where microbiota restoration is clearly superior.
teaching_points: CDI recurrence risk escalates with each episode: approximately 25% after initial episode, 40% after first recurrence, and greater than 60% after second recurrence, making microbiota-based therapy essential for multiply recurrent disease.

FDA-approved microbiota-based products (fecal microbiota live-jslm [Rebyota] and fecal microbiota spores live-brpk [Vowst]) now provide standardized alternatives to conventional FMT, with the 2024 IDSA/SHEA update incorporating these into recurrent CDI management algorithms.

Bezlotoxumab is an adjunctive therapy given as a single IV infusion during antibiotic treatment to reduce CDI recurrence risk by approximately 40%, but it does not treat active infection and should not be used as monotherapy.
summary_points: For multiply recurrent CDI (second recurrence or beyond) after failure of vancomycin taper, FMT or standardized microbiota-based therapy (Rebyota, Vowst) is recommended over additional antibiotic courses per the 2024 IDSA/SHEA focused update.

talk.title: DKA vs HHS: Management Priorities
talk.subtitle: Fluid Resuscitation as the Cornerstone of HHS Management
guideline_sources: ADA Consensus Report on Hyperglycemic Crises 2024
Kitabchi AE et al. Diabetes Care 2009

references.source: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes
Kitabchi AE et al. Hyperglycemic crises in adult patients with diabetes. Diabetes Care
Umpierrez GE, Davis GM. Hyperglycemic crises: management updates. Med Clin North Am

question.stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter after being found lethargic and confused at home. The daughter reports that the patient has had progressive fatigue, increased thirst, and frequent urination over the past 10 days. The patient has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and glipizide, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. She recently had a urinary tract infection treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 2 weeks ago. She does not drink alcohol or use tobacco. Her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, heart rate is 118/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. BMI is 31 kg/m2. On physical examination, she has dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, and is oriented only to person. There is no Kussmaul breathing. Laboratory studies show: Serum glucose: 948 mg/dL Serum sodium: 128 mEq/L (corrected sodium: 142 mEq/L) Serum potassium: 5.1 mEq/L Serum bicarbonate: 22 mEq/L Blood urea nitrogen: 58 mg/dL Serum creatinine: 2.4 mg/dL (baseline 1.3 mg/dL) Serum osmolality: 352 mOsm/kg Arterial blood gas pH: 7.34 Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate: 1.2 mmol/L (normal <0.6 mmol/L) Urinalysis: trace ketones, positive nitrites, positive leukocyte esterase Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management priority?
question.explanation: This patient presents with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS), defined by glucose greater than 600 mg/dL, serum osmolality greater than 320 mOsm/kg, pH greater than 7.30, bicarbonate greater than 18 mEq/L, and altered mental status, with absent or minimal ketosis. Per ADA consensus guidelines, the initial management priority in HHS is aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation (0.9% NaCl at 15-20 mL/kg/hr for the first hour). This differs critically from DKA, where insulin is the cornerstone treatment because the primary pathology is insulin deficiency causing ketoacidosis. In HHS, the primary pathology is profound dehydration (average fluid deficit 8-10 L versus 5-7 L in DKA). Fluid resuscitation alone can reduce glucose by 75-100 mg/dL per hour through dilution and improved renal perfusion. Insulin in HHS should be withheld until potassium is confirmed above 3.3 mEq/L and should be started at lower rates (0.05-0.1 U/kg/hr) only after initial fluid resuscitation, because premature insulin administration can cause rapid osmolality shifts, cerebral edema, and cardiovascular collapse. This patient's potassium of 5.1 mEq/L reflects total body potassium depletion masked by hyperosmolarity and insulin deficiency; aggressive insulin before fluids would cause precipitous hypokalemia. The underlying UTI likely precipitated the crisis. Bicarbonate is not indicated as pH is above 6.9.

wrong_explanations.why: In HHS, insulin is not the initial priority. Premature insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation risks rapid osmolality shifts, cerebral edema, and cardiovascular collapse. Insulin is started only after 1-2 hours of aggressive fluid resuscitation per ADA guidelines.

Subcutaneous insulin is inappropriate for acute hyperglycemic emergencies. HHS requires IV insulin drip for precise dose titration, and only after initial volume resuscitation is established. Subcutaneous absorption is unreliable in dehydrated, hypotensive patients.

Sodium bicarbonate is reserved for DKA with pH less than 6.9, per ADA guidelines. This patient has pH 7.34 and bicarbonate of 22, consistent with HHS without significant acidosis. Bicarbonate administration is not indicated.

Potassium is 5.1 mEq/L, so immediate replacement is not needed. Although total body potassium is depleted, replacement begins when potassium falls below 5.0-5.2 during treatment. Giving potassium at 5.1 risks hyperkalemia, especially with acute kidney injury.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Hyperglycemic crises: DKA vs HHS management priorities

board_pearls: In HHS, the primary pathology is profound dehydration (8-10 L deficit) rather than insulin deficiency; aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation is the initial management priority and alone reduces glucose by 75-100 mg/dL per hour through dilution and restored renal clearance.

Per ADA consensus guidelines, HHS criteria include glucose greater than 600 mg/dL, osmolality greater than 320 mOsm/kg, pH greater than 7.30, bicarbonate greater than 18 mEq/L, and altered sensorium; in contrast, DKA requires pH less than 7.30, bicarbonate less than 18 mEq/L, and significant ketonemia.

The key discriminator between DKA and HHS management: DKA management centers on insulin to reverse ketoacidosis, while HHS management centers on fluid resuscitation to correct hyperosmolarity; premature insulin in HHS causes rapid osmolality shifts and cerebral edema.

Serum potassium in hyperglycemic crises reflects extracellular shifting from hyperosmolarity and insulin deficiency; despite an elevated serum level, total body potassium is depleted by 300-600 mEq, and insulin must be withheld until potassium is confirmed above 3.3 mEq/L per ADA protocol.

The most common wrong-answer trap is selecting immediate insulin bolus for HHS; unlike DKA where insulin corrects the underlying acidosis, in HHS insulin before volume repletion causes hemodynamic instability, hypokalemia, and paradoxical worsening of neurologic status from osmotic shifts.
teaching_points: HHS mortality (10-20%) is higher than DKA (1-5%) largely due to the degree of dehydration and the older, comorbid patient population; aggressive early fluid resuscitation is the most impactful intervention.

Corrected sodium should always be calculated in hyperglycemic crises: add 1.6 mEq/L to measured sodium for every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100; a corrected sodium above 140 suggests severe free water deficit and hyperosmolarity.

An infection is the most common precipitant of both DKA and HHS; always search for and treat the underlying trigger, as hyperglycemic crises will not fully resolve without addressing the precipitating cause.
summary_points: HHS is defined by extreme hyperglycemia (greater than 600 mg/dL), hyperosmolarity (greater than 320 mOsm/kg), and altered mental status without significant ketoacidosis, and its management prioritizes aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation before insulin initiation.

topic: Acute pancreatitis severity — when to escalate to ICU

question.stem: A 54-year-old man is admitted to the hospital because of severe epigastric pain radiating to the back for 12 hours. The pain is constant, rated 9 out of 10, and worsened by eating. He has had 4 episodes of non-bloody emesis. He has a history of alcohol use disorder and drinks approximately 6-8 beers daily for the past 20 years. He denies prior episodes of pancreatitis. He takes no medications. On admission, his temperature is 38.2°C (100.8°F), blood pressure is 88/52 mmHg, heart rate is 118/min, respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. BMI is 34 kg/m2. Physical examination shows significant epigastric tenderness with guarding but no rebound. Bowel sounds are diminished. There is no jaundice. Laboratory studies show: White blood cell count: 18,400/μL Hematocrit: 48% BUN: 32 mg/dL Creatinine: 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL) Serum lipase: 2,840 U/L (reference <60 U/L) Serum calcium: 7.2 mg/dL Serum glucose: 246 mg/dL Serum lactate: 4.8 mmol/L AST: 42 U/L ALT: 38 U/L Total bilirubin: 1.1 mg/dL Arterial blood gas: pH 7.31, PaO2 58 mmHg on room air Chest radiograph shows bilateral basilar atelectasis with small bilateral pleural effusions. Aggressive intravenous crystalloid resuscitation is initiated. Despite 2 liters of lactated Ringer solution over 2 hours, blood pressure remains 90/55 mmHg and oxygen saturation is 90% on 4 liters nasal cannula. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Transfer to the intensive care unit
Urgent CT of the abdomen with contrast
Placement of a nasogastric tube for decompression

question.explanation: Per the Revised Atlanta Classification (2012) and ACG 2013 guidelines, acute pancreatitis is classified as severe when there is persistent organ failure (lasting more than 48 hours) involving one or more organ systems. This patient demonstrates multi-organ dysfunction: cardiovascular failure (persistent hypotension unresponsive to initial fluid resuscitation, requiring vasopressor consideration), respiratory failure (PaO2 58 mmHg on room air, PaO2/FiO2 ratio approximately 276, consistent with acute lung injury; requiring supplemental oxygen with persistent hypoxemia), and renal failure (creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, more than double baseline). The ACG guideline strongly recommends that patients with severe acute pancreatitis be admitted to an ICU or step-down unit. Key severity markers present include SIRS criteria (tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis, fever), elevated BUN and hematocrit (indicators of hemoconcentration and inadequate resuscitation per the BISAP score), hypocalcemia, hyperglycemia, and metabolic acidosis with elevated lactate — satisfying at least 3 Ranson criteria at admission. The persistent hemodynamic instability and hypoxemia despite initial resuscitation mandate ICU transfer for vasopressor support, advanced respiratory monitoring, and goal-directed fluid resuscitation. CT abdomen should be delayed 72-96 hours unless an alternative diagnosis is suspected. ERCP is not indicated without biliary obstruction (normal bilirubin, normal ALT). Prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended per ACG 2013 guidelines. NGT decompression is not standard of care.

wrong_explanations.why: Early CT within 48 hours poorly detects pancreatic necrosis. Per ACG 2013, contrast-enhanced CT should be delayed until 72-96 hours unless diagnostic uncertainty exists or clinical deterioration occurs despite appropriate ICU-level resuscitation.

ERCP is indicated in acute biliary pancreatitis with concurrent cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. This patient has alcoholic pancreatitis with normal bilirubin and transaminases, so ERCP is not indicated.

Per ACG 2013, prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended in acute pancreatitis regardless of severity or predicted degree of necrosis. Antibiotics should be reserved for documented infected necrosis or concurrent infection.

Routine nasogastric decompression provides no benefit in acute pancreatitis per ACG guidelines. It is reserved only for patients with intractable vomiting or ileus with significant gastric distension, not as standard management.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Acute pancreatitis: severity assessment and ICU escalation criteria

board_pearls: Per the Revised Atlanta Classification 2012, severe acute pancreatitis is defined by persistent organ failure (more than 48 hours) — this patient has cardiovascular, respiratory, and renal failure mandating ICU admission for vasopressors, ventilatory support, and aggressive resuscitation.
ACG 2013 strongly recommends ICU or step-down admission for patients meeting criteria for severe pancreatitis; early SIRS with persistent organ failure at 48 hours carries mortality exceeding 30%.

The key discriminator between ICU transfer and CT imaging is timing: organ failure demands immediate escalation, whereas CT for necrosis assessment is optimally performed at 72-96 hours when necrosis has fully demarcated.

Ranson criteria (more than or equal to 3 at admission predicts severe disease), BISAP score (BUN greater than 25, impaired mental status, SIRS, age greater than 60, pleural effusion), and APACHE-II (greater than or equal to 8) are validated severity scoring systems — this patient satisfies multiple criteria across all three systems.

The most common wrong-answer trap is ordering early CT: contrast-enhanced CT within the first 48 hours has poor sensitivity for necrosis and does not change acute management — treat the organ failure first by escalating to ICU-level care.
teaching_points: Persistent organ failure lasting more than 48 hours defines severe acute pancreatitis and mandates ICU admission; transient organ failure resolving within 48 hours is classified as moderately severe.

Goal-directed fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer solution (preferred over normal saline per AGA 2018) at 5-10 mL/kg/hr initially, titrated to urine output, BUN, and hematocrit, is the cornerstone of early management.
ERCP should be performed within 24 hours only in biliary pancreatitis with concurrent cholangitis; prophylactic antibiotics and routine NGT decompression are not recommended.
summary_points: Acute pancreatitis with persistent hypotension, hypoxemia, and acute kidney injury despite initial fluid resuscitation constitutes severe disease requiring immediate ICU transfer for vasopressor support and advanced monitoring.

question.stem: A 38-year-old man presents to the infectious disease clinic for routine follow-up. He was diagnosed with HIV 2 years ago and has been on a regimen of dolutegravir, tenofovir alafenamide, and emtricitabine. His most recent CD4 count is 480 cells/microL, and his HIV RNA viral load is undetectable (<20 copies/mL). He recently immigrated from Ethiopia 6 months ago. A tuberculin skin test placed 48 hours ago shows 12 mm of induration. He denies cough, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. His temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure is 122/78 mmHg, pulse is 72/min, and respirations are 16/min. Physical examination is unremarkable. A chest radiograph shows no infiltrates, cavitations, or lymphadenopathy. Sputum acid-fast bacilli smears are negative. Liver function tests, complete blood count, and basic metabolic panel are within normal limits. The decision is made to treat latent tuberculosis infection. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment regimen?

choices.text: Rifapentine and isoniazid weekly for 3 months
Rifabutin and isoniazid daily for 3 months
Isoniazid and rifampin daily for 3 months

question.explanation: Per CDC/NTCA 2020 guidelines and NIH ART guidelines, the 3HP regimen (once-weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid for 12 weeks) is a preferred short-course regimen for latent TB infection (LTBI) in people with HIV. The critical issue in this patient is drug interaction between rifamycins and antiretrovirals. Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 and UGT1A1 inducer that dramatically reduces dolutegravir levels, making 4-month rifampin (choice A) and 3-month isoniazid-rifampin (choice E) problematic without ART regimen changes. In contrast, rifapentine given once weekly in the 3HP regimen has a clinically manageable interaction with dolutegravir. The DOLPHIN study demonstrated that dolutegravir 50 mg twice daily (dose adjustment) with weekly rifapentine maintains adequate dolutegravir levels. Current NIH guidelines recommend 3HP with dolutegravir-based ART using dolutegravir dose adjustment to 50 mg BID during treatment. This makes 3HP the preferred short-course option. Isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months (choice B) is acceptable but has lower completion rates (approximately 50-60%) compared to 3HP (over 80%), making it less preferred per 2020 CDC guidelines. Rifabutin-isoniazid daily for 3 months (choice D) is not a standard CDC-recommended LTBI regimen. The combination of shorter duration, higher completion rates, and manageable drug interactions with dolutegravir-based ART makes 3HP the most appropriate choice.

wrong_explanations.why: Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4/UGT1A1 inducer that drastically reduces dolutegravir trough concentrations. Daily rifampin necessitates switching ART regimens, making this regimen problematic in patients stable on dolutegravir-based therapy.

Nine months of daily isoniazid is an acceptable LTBI regimen but is less preferred per 2020 CDC guidelines due to significantly lower completion rates (50-60%) compared to 3HP (>80%). Longer regimens increase nonadherence risk.

A 3-month daily rifabutin-isoniazid regimen is not a standard CDC/NTCA-recommended LTBI treatment regimen. Rifabutin is used in active TB treatment to reduce drug interactions, but this specific combination and duration lacks guideline endorsement for LTBI.

Daily rifampin for 3 months with isoniazid poses the same significant drug interaction concern as 4-month rifampin alone. Daily rifampin markedly reduces dolutegravir levels via CYP3A4/UGT1A1 induction, potentially causing virologic failure.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Latent TB treatment in HIV: rifamycin-ART drug interactions

board_pearls: Rifapentine given once weekly in 3HP has a manageable interaction with dolutegravir (dose-adjusted to 50 mg BID), unlike daily rifampin which drastically reduces dolutegravir levels through potent CYP3A4 and UGT1A1 induction.

Per 2020 CDC/NTCA guidelines, 3HP (12-dose weekly rifapentine-isoniazid) is a preferred short-course LTBI regimen for people with HIV, endorsed for use with dolutegravir-based or efavirenz-based ART with appropriate dose adjustments.

The key discriminator between 3HP and rifampin-based regimens in HIV patients on dolutegravir is the FREQUENCY of rifamycin dosing: once-weekly rifapentine allows dolutegravir recovery between doses, while daily rifampin causes sustained enzyme induction and clinically significant drug levels reduction.

The PREVENT TB trial (Sterling et al., NEJM 2011) established 3HP noninferiority to 9-month isoniazid with superior completion rates; the DOLPHIN study confirmed pharmacokinetic safety of 3HP with dose-adjusted dolutegravir in HIV patients.

The most common wrong-answer trap is selecting 9-month isoniazid (avoiding all drug interactions) — while safe, it is less preferred per current guidelines because completion rates are significantly lower than 3HP, reducing real-world effectiveness.
teaching_points: In HIV patients on integrase inhibitor-based ART, rifampin-containing LTBI regimens require ART regimen changes, whereas once-weekly rifapentine in 3HP can be used with dolutegravir dose adjustment (50 mg BID).
TST cutoff for positive result in HIV-positive patients is 5 mm or greater, but this patient clearly meets the threshold at 12 mm regardless of immune status.
Before starting LTBI treatment, active TB must be excluded with symptom review, chest radiograph, and sputum studies — all performed in this vignette.
summary_points: 3HP (once-weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid for 12 weeks) is the preferred short-course LTBI regimen in HIV patients on dolutegravir-based ART, with dolutegravir dose adjustment to 50 mg BID during treatment, offering superior completion rates over 9-month isoniazid and avoiding the problematic daily rifampin-dolutegravir interaction.

talk.title: ITP First-Line Treatment in Pregnancy
talk.subtitle: Management of immune thrombocytopenia during pregnancy

references.source: ASH 2019 Guidelines for Immune Thrombocytopenia
Provan D et al. Updated international consensus report on the investigation and management of primary immune thrombocytopenia. Blood Adv. 2019;3(22):3780-3817

question.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 18 weeks gestation presents to her obstetrician because of easy bruising noticed over the past 3 weeks. She describes new bruises appearing on her arms and legs without trauma, occurring almost daily. She also reports occasional bleeding from her gums when brushing her teeth. She denies epistaxis, hematuria, melena, heavy vaginal bleeding, fever, weight loss, joint pain, or rash. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated to this point. She has no prior history of bleeding disorders or thrombocytopenia. She takes only a prenatal vitamin. She does not drink alcohol or smoke. Her family history is unremarkable. Vital signs are: temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 82/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and SpO2 99% on room air. Physical examination reveals scattered ecchymoses on the bilateral upper and lower extremities and petechiae on the buccal mucosa. There is no hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or joint swelling. The uterus is consistent with an 18-week gestation. Laboratory studies: Hemoglobin: 12.1 g/dL White blood cell count: 7,200/μL with normal differential Platelet count: 22,000/μL Mean platelet volume: 11.2 fL (elevated) Peripheral blood smear: large platelets, no schistocytes, no blasts Prothrombin time: 12.8 seconds (normal) Partial thromboplastin time: 29 seconds (normal) Fibrinogen: 380 mg/dL Lactate dehydrogenase: 168 U/L (normal) AST: 22 U/L ALT: 18 U/L Creatinine: 0.6 mg/dL HIV and hepatitis C antibody: negative Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
question.explanation: Per ASH 2019 guidelines for ITP, corticosteroids are the recommended first-line treatment for ITP requiring therapy in pregnancy. The preferred regimen is prednisone at the lowest effective dose (typically starting at 0.5-1 mg/kg, then tapering). Corticosteroids are preferred over IVIG as initial therapy because they are effective, widely available, and have an established safety profile in pregnancy. IVIG is reserved for cases requiring rapid platelet elevation (e.g., active significant bleeding, preparation for procedures) or when corticosteroids fail or are contraindicated. This patient has symptomatic ITP (mucocutaneous bleeding, platelets 22,000/μL) at 18 weeks gestation, warranting treatment. The diagnosis is supported by isolated thrombocytopenia with large platelets, no schistocytes (excluding TMA/TTP), normal coagulation studies (excluding DIC), normal liver function (excluding HELLP, which occurs later in pregnancy), and negative HIV/HCV. Gestational thrombocytopenia, the most common cause of thrombocytopenia in pregnancy, rarely causes platelets below 70,000/μL and is asymptomatic, making ITP the most likely diagnosis here. Treatment is indicated given platelets below 30,000/μL with mucocutaneous bleeding.

wrong_explanations.why: IVIG is second-line or used when rapid platelet rise is needed (severe bleeding, perioperative). Per ASH 2019, corticosteroids are preferred first-line in pregnant patients with ITP not requiring emergent platelet elevation.

Romiplostim (TPO receptor agonist) lacks sufficient safety data in pregnancy. ASH 2019 suggests TPO-RAs only when other therapies fail. It is not first-line and crosses the placenta with unknown fetal effects.
Rituximab is a category C agent that crosses the placenta, especially in the second and third trimesters, causing neonatal B-cell depletion. It is avoided in pregnancy and is not first-line therapy.

Splenectomy in pregnancy carries significant surgical risks including preterm labor and fetal loss. If needed, it is optimally performed in the second trimester but only after medical therapies fail. It is not first-line.

board_pearls: Corticosteroids (prednisone) are first-line for ITP in pregnancy per ASH 2019 because they are effective, safe in pregnancy, and avoid risks of other agents; use the lowest effective dose and taper to minimize gestational diabetes and hypertension risk.

ASH 2019 recommends treating pregnant patients with ITP when platelets fall below 30,000/μL or when there is clinically significant bleeding; the treatment threshold rises to 50,000/μL near delivery for vaginal birth and 80,000/μL for neuraxial anesthesia.

Gestational thrombocytopenia (the most common cause of low platelets in pregnancy) rarely causes platelets below 70,000/μL, is asymptomatic, and requires no treatment — platelets below 50,000/μL with bleeding symptoms strongly favor ITP over gestational thrombocytopenia.

IVIG is not first-line but is used when a rapid platelet response is required (severe hemorrhage, imminent delivery, or corticosteroid failure); the combination of corticosteroids plus IVIG can be used in emergent situations.

The most common wrong-answer trap is choosing IVIG as first-line: while IVIG works faster, ASH 2019 recommends corticosteroids first due to similar efficacy, lower cost, and established pregnancy safety profile — IVIG is reserved for refractory or emergent situations.
teaching_points: In pregnant patients with ITP, the treatment threshold is generally platelets below 30,000/μL or symptomatic bleeding; corticosteroids are first-line, and IVIG is second-line or for emergent situations.
Key distinguishing features of ITP from gestational thrombocytopenia include platelet count below 70,000/μL, onset in the first or second trimester, and presence of bleeding symptoms.

Rituximab, TPO receptor agonists, and splenectomy are avoided or used only as last resort in pregnancy due to fetal risks; among these, splenectomy is safest if performed in the second trimester when absolutely necessary.
summary_points: Corticosteroids are first-line treatment for ITP in pregnancy per ASH 2019 guidelines; IVIG is reserved for emergent or refractory cases; rituximab, TPO-RAs, and splenectomy carry significant fetal risks and are not appropriate initial therapy.

talk.title: Wake-Up Stroke and Extended Thrombectomy Window
talk.subtitle: DAWN/DEFUSE 3 criteria for late-presenting large vessel occlusion
guideline_sources: AHA/ASA 2019 Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

references.source: Powers WJ et al. Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke. Stroke. 2019;50:e344-e418.
Nogueira RG et al. Thrombectomy 6 to 24 Hours after Stroke with a Mismatch between Deficit and Infarct (DAWN). N Engl J Med. 2018;378:11-21.
Albers GW et al. Thrombectomy for Stroke at 6 to 16 Hours with Selection by Perfusion Imaging (DEFUSE 3). N Engl J Med. 2018;378:708-718.
Ma H et al. Thrombolysis Guided by Perfusion Imaging up to 9 Hours after Onset of Stroke (EXTEND). N Engl J Med. 2019;380:1795-1803.

question.stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband after he found her on the floor with right-sided weakness and inability to speak at 7:00 AM. She was last seen normal when she went to bed at 10:00 PM the previous night. Her medical history includes hypertension treated with amlodipine and atrial fibrillation for which she takes apixaban. She had discontinued apixaban on her own 3 weeks ago due to cost. Her vital signs are temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 168/92 mmHg, heart rate 88/min and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. On examination, she has a dense right hemiplegia, global aphasia, right-sided neglect, and forced left gaze deviation. Her National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score is 19. Point-of-care glucose is 142 mg/dL. Non-contrast CT of the head shows no hemorrhage and no early ischemic changes. CT angiography demonstrates a left middle cerebral artery M1 segment occlusion. CT perfusion imaging reveals a large area of critically hypoperfused tissue (Tmax >6 seconds volume of 85 mL) with a small ischemic core (cerebral blood flow <30% volume of 12 mL), yielding a mismatch ratio of approximately 7:1. The time from last known well is approximately 9 hours. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Aspirin and clopidogrel dual antiplatelet therapy

question.explanation: Per AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines (Class IIb, Level B for mechanical thrombectomy 6-24 hours from last known well with DAWN/DEFUSE 3 selection criteria), mechanical thrombectomy is recommended for eligible patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) in the anterior circulation who present 6-24 hours from last known well, provided they meet DAWN or DEFUSE 3 selection criteria based on clinical-imaging mismatch. This patient has an LVO (left M1 occlusion), a severe deficit (NIHSS 19), a small ischemic core (12 mL), and a large penumbral mismatch ratio (7:1), satisfying both DAWN criteria (clinical deficit disproportionate to infarct core) and DEFUSE 3 criteria (target mismatch with core 6 seconds volume >15 mL, and mismatch ratio ≥1.8). DAWN enrolled patients 6-24 hours from last known well using clinical-core mismatch on CT perfusion or DWI-MRI; DEFUSE 3 enrolled patients 6-16 hours using perfusion imaging mismatch. Both trials demonstrated significant benefit of thrombectomy over medical therapy (DAWN: 90-day mRS 0-2 in 49% vs 13%; DEFUSE 3: 45% vs 17%). IV alteplase alone is insufficient for LVO and is outside the 4.5-hour window from last known well. Dual antiplatelet therapy addresses secondary prevention for minor stroke or TIA, not acute LVO. IV heparin is not indicated acutely in ischemic stroke. Watchful waiting with delayed reimaging would allow salvageable penumbra to infarct.

wrong_explanations.why: IV alteplase is contraindicated beyond 4.5 hours from last known well per AHA/ASA 2019. Furthermore, alteplase alone is insufficient to recanalize a proximal M1 occlusion and would not substitute for thrombectomy.

Dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) is indicated per CHANCE/POINT trials for minor stroke (NIHSS ≤3) or high-risk TIA within 24 hours of onset. This patient has a severe LVO stroke (NIHSS 19) requiring emergent revascularization.

IV heparin is not recommended for acute ischemic stroke treatment per AHA/ASA guidelines. Anticoagulation does not achieve revascularization for proximal LVO and increases hemorrhagic transformation risk.

Delaying intervention allows irreversible conversion of salvageable penumbra to infarct. The imaging already demonstrates favorable mismatch meeting DAWN/DEFUSE 3 criteria, so proceeding immediately to thrombectomy is indicated.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Extended-window thrombectomy for wake-up stroke: DAWN and DEFUSE 3 criteria

board_pearls: DAWN and DEFUSE 3 extended mechanical thrombectomy to 24 and 16 hours respectively by selecting patients with clinical-imaging mismatch (small ischemic core relative to large perfusion deficit or severe clinical deficit), reflecting salvageable penumbral tissue.

AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines give a Class IIb, Level B recommendation for thrombectomy in patients meeting DAWN or DEFUSE 3 criteria with anterior circulation LVO presenting 6-24 hours from last known well.

DAWN uses clinical-core mismatch (NIHSS versus ischemic core volume stratified by age), while DEFUSE 3 uses automated perfusion imaging mismatch (ratio ≥1.8, core 15 mL); both require CT perfusion or diffusion-weighted MRI for patient selection.

The EXTEND trial separately demonstrated that IV alteplase guided by perfusion imaging mismatch could extend the thrombolysis window to 4.5-9 hours, but this applies to non-LVO strokes and patients with smaller infarcts; proximal LVO patients like this one require thrombectomy regardless.

A common trap is selecting IV alteplase for wake-up stroke patients with LVO: alteplase alone has poor recanalization rates for proximal occlusions, and the standard 4.5-hour window from last known well has passed; thrombectomy is the definitive intervention.
teaching_points: Wake-up strokes and unknown-onset strokes can be treated with mechanical thrombectomy up to 24 hours from last known well if perfusion imaging demonstrates a small ischemic core with a large mismatch, per DAWN and DEFUSE 3 trial criteria.
The key imaging parameters for extended-window thrombectomy include ischemic core volume (6 seconds penumbral volume exceeding core by >15 mL.

IV alteplase remains limited to 4.5 hours from last known well for standard use; the EXTEND trial extended alteplase to 9 hours using perfusion mismatch in selected patients without large core infarcts, but this does not replace the need for thrombectomy in large vessel occlusion.
summary_points: In patients with wake-up stroke or unknown onset presenting 6-24 hours from last known well with anterior circulation large vessel occlusion and favorable perfusion imaging mismatch (small core, large penumbra), mechanical thrombectomy is the standard of care per DAWN and DEFUSE 3, endorsed by AHA/ASA 2019 guidelines as Class IIb, Level B.

topic: Gout flare during anticoagulation — treatment choice

talk.title: Gout Flare Management During Anticoagulation
talk.subtitle: Acute gout treatment selection in a patient on therapeutic warfarin
guideline_sources: ACR 2020 Guidelines for Management of Gout

references.source: FitzGerald JD, et al. 2020 American College of Rheumatology Guideline for Management of Gout. Arthritis Care Res.
White WB, et al. Cardiovascular Safety of Febuxostat or Allopurinol in Patients with Gout (CARES). N Engl J Med.

question.stem: A 71-year-old man presents to the clinic because of acute left first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint pain and swelling that began 18 hours ago. He describes the pain as severe (9/10), throbbing, and constant, worsened by any weight bearing. He has not had any recent trauma. His medical history includes atrial fibrillation for which he takes warfarin, hypertension treated with lisinopril, and a prior episode of gout in the same joint 8 months ago that resolved with indomethacin. He also takes a daily aspirin. He drinks 2-3 beers per week and does not smoke. His temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F), blood pressure is 142/84 mmHg, heart rate is 78 bpm and irregularly irregular, respiratory rate is 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical examination shows an erythematous, markedly swollen, and exquisitely tender left first MTP joint with limited range of motion. No other joints are involved. Laboratory studies show: Serum creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL Serum uric acid: 8.9 mg/dL INR: 2.8 (therapeutic range 2.0-3.0) White blood cell count: 9,800/microL Platelet count: 210,000/microL Arthrocentesis of the left first MTP joint reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals with no organisms on Gram stain. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's acute gout flare?
question.explanation: Per the ACR 2020 Guideline for Management of Gout, first-line therapies for acute gout flares include NSAIDs, colchicine, or glucocorticoids (oral, intra-articular, or intramuscular). Selection among these agents depends on patient-specific contraindications and drug interactions. In this patient on therapeutic warfarin (INR 2.8), NSAIDs are contraindicated because they inhibit platelet function and increase bleeding risk, and they potentiate warfarin's anticoagulant effect by displacing it from albumin and inhibiting CYP2C9. Colchicine, while not inherently contraindicated with warfarin, has a clinically significant drug interaction: colchicine can increase INR by inhibiting CYP3A4-mediated warfarin metabolism and reducing intestinal P-glycoprotein activity, raising supratherapeutic anticoagulation risk. Its narrow therapeutic index and gastrointestinal toxicity further complicate use in this setting. Oral prednisone is the safest and most appropriate choice. It effectively treats monoarticular gout flares, has no significant interaction with warfarin, and does not increase bleeding risk. A typical regimen is prednisone 30-40 mg daily for 5-7 days with taper. Intra-articular triamcinolone is an alternative for monoarticular flares but performing joint injection in an anticoagulated patient with a supratherapeutic INR carries procedural bleeding risk, making oral prednisone preferable. Allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy for chronic management and does not treat acute flares; initiating it without anti-inflammatory prophylaxis can worsen the current flare.

wrong_explanations.why: NSAIDs are contraindicated with therapeutic anticoagulation. Indomethacin inhibits platelet function, potentiates warfarin via CYP2C9 inhibition, and significantly increases GI and systemic bleeding risk when INR is already therapeutic.

Colchicine interacts with warfarin, potentially raising INR to supratherapeutic levels. Its narrow therapeutic index and GI side effects make it less safe than corticosteroids in anticoagulated patients, per ACR 2020 guidance to individualize based on contraindications.

While intra-articular corticosteroid injection is effective for monoarticular gout, performing arthrocentesis and injection in a patient with therapeutic anticoagulation (INR 2.8) carries hemarthrosis risk. Oral prednisone is equally effective without procedural bleeding concern.

Allopurinol is urate-lowering therapy for long-term gout management. It does not treat acute inflammation and, if started during a flare without anti-inflammatory prophylaxis, can paradoxically worsen the acute episode by mobilizing urate crystals.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Acute gout flare treatment in anticoagulated patients

board_pearls: Oral corticosteroids are the preferred treatment for acute gout in anticoagulated patients because they lack platelet inhibition, do not potentiate warfarin, and carry no procedural bleeding risk — per ACR 2020 recommendation to select among NSAIDs, colchicine, or steroids based on patient-specific contraindications.

ACR 2020 conditionally recommends NSAIDs, colchicine, or glucocorticoids as first-line for acute gout but emphasizes individualization; in anticoagulated patients, glucocorticoids are preferred because NSAIDs increase bleeding and colchicine raises INR via drug interaction.

The discriminating feature between oral prednisone and intra-articular injection in this scenario is that procedural injection into an anticoagulated joint (INR 2.8) risks hemarthrosis, while oral prednisone achieves equivalent efficacy without procedural risk for a single-joint flare.

The ACR 2020 guideline recommends starting urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol first-line, target uric acid less than 6 mg/dL) even during an acute flare, but only with concomitant anti-inflammatory prophylaxis for 3-6 months — allopurinol alone worsens acute flares.

The most common wrong-answer trap is choosing indomethacin because NSAIDs are classic first-line gout therapy; however, in anticoagulated patients, NSAIDs are contraindicated due to synergistic bleeding risk, CYP2C9 inhibition of warfarin metabolism, and platelet dysfunction.
teaching_points: In anticoagulated patients with acute gout, oral corticosteroids are the safest first-line option because they avoid NSAID-related bleeding risk and colchicine-warfarin drug interactions.
Intra-articular injection is relatively contraindicated when INR is supratherapeutic or at the upper end of the therapeutic range due to risk of hemarthrosis.
Allopurinol may be initiated during an acute flare per ACR 2020 guidelines, but only with concurrent anti-inflammatory prophylaxis — it should never be used alone to treat an acute episode.
summary_points: Oral prednisone is the treatment of choice for acute gout in patients on therapeutic warfarin because it avoids NSAID-related bleeding potentiation, colchicine-warfarin drug interactions, and procedural bleeding risk from intra-articular injection.
