topic: Hepatitis B reactivation prophylaxis before chemo

talk.title: Hepatitis B Reactivation Prophylaxis
talk.subtitle: HBV screening and antiviral prophylaxis before immunosuppressive therapy
guideline_sources: ASCO 2015 Provisional Clinical Opinion on HBV Screening

references.source: AASLD 2018 Hepatitis B Guidance: Prevention, Diagnosis, Treatment
AGA Clinical Practice Guideline on Prevention of HBV Reactivation
ASCO Provisional Clinical Opinion Update: HBV Screening Prior to Cytotoxic Chemotherapy

question.stem: A 58-year-old woman is evaluated in the oncology clinic for newly diagnosed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. She is scheduled to begin R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) chemotherapy in 2 weeks. She was born in South Korea and immigrated to the United States at age 30. She has no history of liver disease, jaundice, or prior antiviral therapy. She takes lisinopril for hypertension. She does not drink alcohol or use tobacco. Her vital signs are normal. Physical examination reveals bilateral cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy; there is no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or ascites. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglobin: 11.2 g/dL Platelet count: 185,000/microL AST: 24 U/L ALT: 28 U/L Total bilirubin: 0.8 mg/dL Albumin: 3.8 g/dL Creatinine: 0.9 mg/dL HBsAg: negative Anti-HBs: positive Anti-HBc (total): positive HBV DNA: undetectable Anti-HCV: negative Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management regarding hepatitis B?

choices.text: Tenofovir treatment after HBV DNA becomes detectable

question.explanation: Per AASLD 2018 and AGA 2015 guidelines, all patients should be screened for HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc) before initiating immunosuppressive therapy. This patient has resolved HBV infection (HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive, anti-HBs-positive, undetectable HBV DNA). Rituximab, an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, carries the highest risk of HBV reactivation among immunosuppressive agents (greater than 10% reactivation risk), even in patients with resolved infection. AASLD 2018 recommends antiviral prophylaxis for all patients receiving anti-CD20 therapy regardless of HBsAg status if anti-HBc is positive. Prophylaxis should begin before or simultaneously with immunosuppression and continue for at least 12 months after the last dose of rituximab. Entecavir or tenofovir are preferred due to high potency and high barrier to resistance. Lamivudine has a low barrier to resistance and is no longer preferred, particularly for prolonged courses. A preemptive monitoring strategy (treating only after HBV DNA becomes detectable) is inferior to prophylaxis in high-risk settings like rituximab use, as reactivation can be fulminant. Vaccination is unnecessary since anti-HBs is already positive, and it would not prevent reactivation from cccDNA in hepatocytes. The presence of normal transaminases and undetectable HBV DNA does not eliminate reactivation risk.

wrong_explanations.why: Resolved HBV (anti-HBc-positive) patients receiving rituximab-based regimens have greater than 10% reactivation risk. AASLD 2018 strongly recommends antiviral prophylaxis in this setting, not observation alone.

A preemptive monitoring strategy (waiting for detectable HBV DNA) is not recommended with rituximab because reactivation can be rapid and fulminant. Prophylaxis is superior to preemptive therapy per AGA 2015 and AASLD 2018 guidelines.

This patient already has anti-HBs positivity indicating immunity. Vaccination does not prevent reactivation, which originates from covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA) persisting in hepatocytes despite serologic resolution.

Lamivudine has a low genetic barrier to resistance (up to 70% at 5 years). AASLD 2018 recommends entecavir or tenofovir as preferred agents for prophylaxis, especially when prolonged courses are anticipated with rituximab.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Hepatitis B reactivation prophylaxis with immunosuppressive therapy

board_pearls: Rituximab depletes B cells and allows HBV reactivation from intrahepatic cccDNA even in HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive patients with resolved infection, making prophylaxis mandatory per AASLD 2018.

AASLD 2018 recommends universal HBV screening (HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc) before immunosuppressive therapy and antiviral prophylaxis for all anti-HBc-positive patients receiving anti-CD20 agents, continued for at least 12 months post-rituximab.

The key discriminator between prophylaxis and monitoring is the agent: rituximab and other anti-CD20 therapies require prophylaxis, whereas conventional chemotherapy without rituximab in resolved HBV may allow a monitoring strategy with serial HBV DNA.

AGA 2015 stratifies reactivation risk: anti-CD20 agents are highest risk (greater than 10%), anthracyclines and moderate-dose corticosteroids are moderate risk (1-10%), and low-dose methotrexate and azathioprine are low risk (less than 1%).

The most common wrong-answer trap is choosing lamivudine because it is a familiar antiviral; however, its high resistance rate makes it inferior to entecavir or tenofovir for prolonged prophylaxis courses required with rituximab.
teaching_points: All patients starting immunosuppressive therapy should be screened with HBsAg, anti-HBs, and anti-HBc before treatment initiation.

Anti-CD20 agents (rituximab, ofatumumab, obinutuzumab) carry the highest risk of HBV reactivation and require antiviral prophylaxis even in patients with resolved infection (HBsAg-negative, anti-HBc-positive).
Entecavir and tenofovir are preferred over lamivudine for HBV prophylaxis due to superior resistance profiles, especially for prolonged courses.
summary_points: Resolved HBV infection plus rituximab-based chemotherapy mandates antiviral prophylaxis with entecavir or tenofovir, beginning before immunosuppression and continuing at least 12 months after the last rituximab dose.

topic: Asthma exacerbation — when to escalate to MgSO4

talk.title: Asthma Exacerbation: Escalation to IV Magnesium Sulfate
talk.subtitle: Severe acute asthma refractory to initial bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy
guideline_sources: GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention
BTS/SIGN British Guideline on the Management of Asthma 2019

references.source: GINA 2024 Global Strategy for Asthma Management and Prevention
Goodacre S et al. 3Mg Trial. Lancet Respir Med 2013;1:293-300
Rowe BH et al. Magnesium sulfate for treating exacerbations of acute asthma in the emergency department. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2000
NAEPP Expert Panel Report 3 (EPR-3)

question.stem: A 32-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of worsening shortness of breath and wheezing for 6 hours. She has a history of poorly controlled persistent asthma with two prior hospitalizations for asthma exacerbations in the past year. Her current medications include fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 mcg twice daily and albuterol as needed. She reports using her rescue inhaler every 1-2 hours today without improvement. She denies fever, cough productive of purulent sputum, or recent upper respiratory symptoms. She does not smoke and has no known drug allergies. On arrival, her temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), blood pressure is 128/78 mmHg, heart rate is 122/min, respiratory rate is 32/min, and oxygen saturation is 89% on room air. She is sitting upright, using accessory muscles of respiration, and speaking in 2- to 3-word sentences. Lung examination reveals diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezes with a prolonged expiratory phase and poor air movement. She is started on continuous nebulized albuterol, ipratropium bromide nebulization, intravenous methylprednisolone 125 mg, and supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula. After 60 minutes of continuous nebulized bronchodilator therapy, her respiratory rate remains 30/min, heart rate is 118/min, oxygen saturation is 91% on 4 L/min nasal cannula, and she continues to speak in short phrases only. Peak expiratory flow is 28% of predicted. Arterial blood gas on 4 L/min shows pH 7.38, PaCO2 40 mmHg, and PaO2 68 mmHg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
question.explanation: Per GINA 2024 and NAEPP EPR-3, intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g over 20 minutes) is recommended as adjunctive therapy in severe asthma exacerbations that remain refractory to initial intensive bronchodilator and systemic corticosteroid therapy. This patient meets criteria for a severe exacerbation: accessory muscle use, inability to speak in full sentences, PEF less than 25-30% predicted, tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxemia despite treatment. Critically, her PaCO2 of 40 mmHg — which appears normal — is actually ominous during a severe exacerbation because hyperventilation should produce hypocapnia; a normalizing PaCO2 suggests respiratory muscle fatigue and impending respiratory failure. Magnesium sulfate acts as a smooth muscle relaxant by inhibiting calcium influx into airway smooth muscle cells. The Cochrane review by Rowe et al. demonstrated that IV MgSO4 reduces hospital admissions in severe exacerbations (PEF less than 25-30% predicted) unresponsive to initial therapy. GINA 2024 recommends IV MgSO4 as an add-on in patients with severe exacerbations not responding to first-hour treatment. This patient has already received continuous nebulized albuterol, ipratropium, and systemic steroids for 60 minutes without adequate improvement, making IV MgSO4 the appropriate escalation before considering mechanical ventilatory support. She is not yet in frank respiratory failure requiring intubation — she is still protecting her airway and maintaining adequate gas exchange, albeit tenuously.

wrong_explanations.why: Subcutaneous terbutaline is a second-line beta-agonist option occasionally used if nebulization is ineffective due to poor air movement, but IV MgSO4 has stronger evidence for benefit in severe refractory exacerbations per GINA 2024 and should be given first.

IV aminophylline (theophylline) is no longer recommended for acute asthma exacerbations per GINA 2024 due to lack of additional bronchodilator benefit over standard therapy and significant risk of toxicity including arrhythmias and seizures.

Noninvasive positive pressure ventilation has limited evidence in acute asthma and is not a standard recommendation per GINA 2024 for asthma exacerbations. It is first-line for hypercapnic COPD exacerbations (per Brochard et al.) but not routinely applied in acute asthma.

Intubation is reserved for patients with impending or actual respiratory arrest, altered mental status, or progressive hypercapnic respiratory failure despite maximal therapy. This patient is still alert and maintaining her airway; escalation with MgSO4 should be attempted first.

abim_classification.specific_topic: Asthma exacerbation: escalation to IV magnesium sulfate

board_pearls: IV magnesium sulfate (2 g over 20 min) relaxes airway smooth muscle by inhibiting calcium influx and is indicated in severe asthma exacerbations (PEF less than 25-30% predicted) refractory to 60 minutes of continuous beta-agonists, ipratropium, and systemic corticosteroids.
GINA 2024 recommends IV MgSO4 as adjunctive therapy for severe exacerbations not responding to initial intensive treatment; it is NOT recommended for mild-moderate exacerbations.

A normal PaCO2 (40 mmHg) during a severe asthma exacerbation is an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure — expected value should be low (25-35 mmHg) due to hyperventilation; this discriminates severe from moderate exacerbations.

The Cochrane systematic review (Rowe et al.) and 3Mg trial demonstrated that IV MgSO4 reduces hospital admissions specifically in severe exacerbations with PEF less than 25-30% predicted, but not in mild-moderate exacerbations.

IV aminophylline is the most common wrong-answer trap; it was formerly used in acute asthma but is no longer recommended by GINA or NAEPP due to lack of additional bronchodilator benefit and high toxicity risk (arrhythmias, seizures, nausea).
teaching_points: The stepwise escalation for severe asthma exacerbations is: continuous nebulized SABA plus ipratropium plus systemic corticosteroids as initial therapy, then IV magnesium sulfate if refractory after 60 minutes, then consider terbutaline or epinephrine for impending arrest, and intubation as a last resort.

A normalizing or rising PaCO2 during a severe asthma exacerbation indicates respiratory muscle fatigue and impending ventilatory failure — do not be falsely reassured by a 'normal' blood gas in this context.
IV MgSO4 benefits are most pronounced in patients with PEF less than 25-30% predicted; there is no demonstrated benefit in mild-moderate exacerbations, making patient selection critical.
summary_points: In severe refractory asthma exacerbations (PEF less than 25-30% predicted, persistent symptoms after 60 minutes of continuous SABA, ipratropium, and systemic steroids), IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes is the recommended next escalation step per GINA 2024.

question.stem: A 34-year-old woman comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance visit. She has no specific complaints. She denies fatigue, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, or menstrual irregularities. She and her husband have been actively trying to conceive for the past 3 months without success. Her medical history is notable for type 1 diabetes mellitus, well controlled on an insulin pump with a hemoglobin A1c of 6.8%. She takes no other medications. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Her mother was diagnosed with Hashimoto thyroiditis at age 40. Vital signs are: temperature 36.8°C (98.2°F), blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, heart rate 72/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and BMI 23 kg/m². Physical examination reveals a non-tender, normal-sized thyroid gland without palpable nodules. The remainder of the examination is unremarkable. Laboratory studies: TSH: 7.8 mIU/L (normal 0.4–4.0) Free T4: 1.1 ng/dL (normal 0.8–1.8) Anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies: positive (elevated) Hemoglobin: 13.2 g/dL Serum creatinine: 0.8 mg/dL Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.text: Reassurance and recheck TSH in 6 months
Repeat TSH in 2 to 3 months before treatment

question.explanation: Per ATA 2017 pregnancy/preconception guidelines, levothyroxine is recommended for women who are actively attempting pregnancy and have subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal free T4), particularly when anti-TPO antibodies are positive. This patient has TSH 7.8 mIU/L with normal free T4, positive anti-TPO antibodies, and is actively trying to conceive — meeting clear criteria for treatment. Untreated subclinical hypothyroidism in pregnancy is associated with increased risk of miscarriage, preterm delivery, and impaired fetal neurodevelopment. The ATA 2017 guideline recommends a preconception TSH goal of less than 2.5 mIU/L. Additionally, her type 1 diabetes places her at higher risk for autoimmune thyroid disease, reinforcing the importance of screening and treatment. Per ATA/AACE 2012 guidelines, treatment is also generally favored when TSH exceeds 10 mIU/L regardless of pregnancy status, but in the preconception setting, treatment is indicated even at lower TSH elevations (above the upper limit of normal). Delaying treatment to recheck TSH would be inappropriate given active conception attempts. Thyroid ultrasound is not indicated without nodularity or goiter. Radioactive iodine uptake is used to evaluate hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism, and is contraindicated in pregnancy or those planning pregnancy.

wrong_explanations.why: Watchful waiting is reasonable for subclinical hypothyroidism in non-pregnant adults with TSH below 10, but is inappropriate in a woman actively trying to conceive, where untreated disease increases miscarriage and fetal developmental risks.
Thyroid ultrasound is indicated for evaluation of palpable nodules or goiter. This patient has a normal-sized, non-nodular gland, so imaging is not warranted and does not address the TSH elevation.
Radioactive iodine uptake evaluates hyperthyroidism, not hypothyroidism. It is also absolutely contraindicated in women who are pregnant or planning pregnancy due to fetal thyroid ablation risk.

While repeating TSH in 2-3 months may be appropriate in asymptomatic non-pregnant patients, delaying treatment in a woman actively attempting conception risks adverse obstetric and fetal outcomes per ATA 2017 guidelines.

board_pearls: Subclinical hypothyroidism in women actively trying to conceive warrants levothyroxine treatment per ATA 2017 guidelines, with a preconception TSH target below 2.5 mIU/L, because untreated disease increases miscarriage and impairs fetal neurodevelopment.

Per ATA/AACE 2012 guidelines, treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism is recommended when TSH exceeds 10 mIU/L in the general population; for TSH 4.5-10, treatment is favored when symptoms, positive anti-TPO antibodies, or pregnancy intent are present.

The key discriminator between treating and observing subclinical hypothyroidism is pregnancy intent — a woman actively trying to conceive should be treated even at mildly elevated TSH levels, unlike an asymptomatic elderly patient where the TRUST trial showed no benefit.

The TRUST trial (2017) demonstrated that levothyroxine for subclinical hypothyroidism in adults aged 65 or older with TSH 4.6-19.9 did not improve symptoms or quality of life, underscoring the age-dependent treatment threshold.

The most common wrong-answer trap is choosing to recheck TSH and observe — this is reasonable in non-pregnant, asymptomatic patients but inappropriate in the preconception setting where delays carry obstetric and developmental risk.
teaching_points: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as elevated TSH with normal free T4. Treatment decisions depend on TSH level, symptom burden, anti-TPO antibody status, age, and pregnancy status.
Type 1 diabetes confers increased risk for autoimmune thyroid disease (polyglandular autoimmune syndrome type 2), making thyroid function screening essential in this population.

In elderly patients (over age 65-70), subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH below 10 generally does not benefit from treatment per the TRUST trial, and overtreatment risks atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis.
summary_points: Treat subclinical hypothyroidism with levothyroxine in women planning pregnancy (target TSH below 2.5), when TSH exceeds 10 in any patient, or when TSH is 4.5-10 with symptoms or positive anti-TPO antibodies in younger patients. Observation is appropriate in asymptomatic elderly patients with mildly elevated TSH.
